description: Known answers for measuring the card checker. 'leak' cases are earlier versions of card text (or the current text, where it still leaks); 'ok' cases are current text the story supports. 'para' is the paragraph after which the text first shows.

cases.text: Sherlock Holmes, Watson's companion, about to leave for Dartmoor.
cases.why: Dartmoor is first named at ¶3; 'Sherlock' at ¶7

cases.text: Sherlock Holmes, Watson's companion, who says at breakfast that he shall have to go.
The other two King's Pyland horses
cases.why: four horses in all; that two of them are Silver Blaze and Bayard is not told until ¶28

cases.text: The chaff-cutting loft
Lord Backwater's larger training establishment, about two miles across the moor (to the west, as seen from King's Pyland), managed by Silas Brown.
cases.why: ¶19 puts Tavistock to the west, not Mapleton (that is ¶69)

cases.text: Opium is put into Hunter's supper
John Straker dies
cases.why: the trainer is first named at ¶10

cases.text: The favourite
Straker's small villa, about two hundred yards from the stables.
Silver Blaze is gone from his stall
Swinging in the hand of the fierce-looking elderly man who strides out from the Mapleton gate.
The favourite's trainer dies
Gypsies: Romani travellers, who camped on moors and commons. The story repeats the period's prejudice that they are thieves who flee the police.
cases.why: says what the story will go on to say about them (Holmes's view comes much later)

cases.text: Dartmoor: A high, wild moorland in Devon, with granite tors, bogs, scattered farms and old tin-mine workings. Doyle's geography is loose: Tavistock is on its western edge, not its middle.
cases.why: comments on how the story places Tavistock, which it does at ¶47; Tavistock is not even mentioned until ¶19

cases.text: A.D.P. briar-root pipe: A pipe of briar root, the usual material. The story does not explain the initials.
cases.why: a claim about what the rest of the story will (not) say

cases.text: On a night with no wind a coat cannot be blown onto a bush: if it hangs there, someone put it there.
cases.why: design question for the user: should a general fact that applies to an event the story has not told yet wait? Haiku says leak ('applies to this story's coat, not yet introduced')

cases.text: Field-glass: Binoculars.
Isonomy: A real and very famous racehorse (foaled 1875), twice winner of the Ascot Gold Cup. To be 'of the Isonomy stock' is to come from a champion's bloodline.
cases.why: real-world fact about a real horse

cases.text: The overcoat is put on the furze-bush
cases.why: ¶93 already says 'the furze-bush upon which the coat had been hung' (my first expectation was wrong; the checker found it)

cases.text: Hunter's supper is drugged
Within thirty yards of the stables a man stops Edith
cases.why: the label said 'Thirty yards from'; the story says 'within thirty yards' (Haiku caught it)

cases.text: Fitzroy Simpson
cases.why: Simpson is named at ¶14 as the man arrested, but nothing yet says he is the man who stopped Edith (¶39–40)

cases.text: Silver Blaze
cases.why: at ¶197 the story itself presents the bay as Silver Blaze ('This must be he', ¶196 — both models rightly passed it there); from ¶198 the owner denies it, and the truth comes at ¶202

cases.text: The long hollow towards Mapleton
cases.why: that is a different hollow (¶116); this card is the bowl-shaped one where the body lay
